answers.answer: A key identifies an entry and retrieves its associated value. Use a namespace for settings plus tenant ID plus device ID, with a separator forbidden in the parts or consistently escaped; for example settings|tenantA|device7 where each part cannot contain |. Store the complete settings record as the value because the lookup reads them together. Including tenant prevents repeating device IDs from colliding, and settings separates status records. This is authoritative because the application treats it as its source of truth, whereas a cache is a disposable copy elsewhere. Key-value access alone does not establish crash survival; persistence settings and failure guarantees need checking. Replacement puts first store {mode: quiet, color: green}, then replace it with {mode: loud}; get returns {mode: loud}, with color gone. Delete removes it; a get observing the deletion reports absent. A timeout only means no result arrived, not absence, and should not trigger replacement data as if the record were missing. Verify permission to the tenant and record independently; a guessed or possessed key only selects data.

evidence.quote: The key-value label says nothing by itself about whether acknowledged writes survive a crash.
An empty value is not necessarily an absent entry.
In a replacement API, putting {mode: quiet, color: green}, then {mode: loud}, leaves only {mode: loud}. The old color field is gone.
A get timeout means no result arrived. It does not tell you whether the key exists.
A separator is safe only if values cannot contain it or are escaped consistently.
A key selects data; it does not grant permission.

answers.answer: Basic lookup requires a known equipment ID. Having region inside the value does not create a lookup to discover IDs with region west. A scan examines entries and filters values, so work grows with entries inspected even if west matches are few; filtering does not erase the reads. An index maps region to matching IDs, finding candidates without inspecting every value, then fetching needed records. It adds storage and update work: changing a region or deleting equipment must update index entries too. Check who maintains it and when writes become visible in index results; application maintenance requires coordination. Basic key-value access does not promise indexes or ordered queries, so verify actual product support.

evidence.quote: Storing the city inside each value does not create an efficient lookup by city.
Its work grows with the entries inspected, even if few match. Filtering the results does not undo the reads already performed.
Maintains another lookup, such as city to matching record IDs.
When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too.
Some stores supply indexes or ordered range queries; basic key-value access promises neither.

answers.answer: Both blind puts write 21, so final count is 21 rather than the intended 22: one increment is lost. With the conditional operation, both submit count 21 conditioned on version 7. One succeeds and advances the version, for example to 8. The other condition now fails and its stale 21 is not written. The rejected worker rereads 21 and the current version, recomputes 22 and conditionally writes against that version, advancing it on success. It bounds retries if others keep winning. A separate version check and unconditional put allow another change in the gap; the test and write must be indivisible in the store to exclude that race. This protection covers the specified atomic scope, not automatically multiple keys or external actions.

evidence.quote: Both writes can succeed, but the final count is 11 instead of 12. One intended increment is lost.
Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation.
The rejected caller rereads the current value and version, recomputes its change and makes another conditional attempt.
Checking the version in a separate request before an unconditional put leaves the same race.

answers.answer: A timeout leaves execution outcome unknown: the write may have finished and only its reply was lost. Repeating an identical replacement with no intervening write leaves the same final value. Repeating an add-one operation can add twice if the first completed, even when each increment is atomic. To avoid duplicate effects, retain the same logical operation ID and intent on retries and coordinate recording the ID with changing data atomically, retaining duplicate records for the retry window. An ID alone is insufficient; verify product scope and support. Without verified duplicate protection, reconcile through application recovery instead of blindly retrying the increment. Use bounded retry/backoff for retryable failures. If another writer intervenes, an unconditional replacement retry could overwrite its newer data, requiring documented conditions or operation identity. TTL expires an entry by a time rule; eviction removes entries for capacity under policy and can occur before TTL. TTL thus does not promise retention, removal does not fetch a refreshed value, and expiration does not schedule business work at the exact deadline. A cache may reload from its source; authoritative data needs retention and recovery planning. Enforce use deadlines during authorization and choose a work-execution mechanism for timed work. Check TTL support, when expired data stops being returned versus physical deletion, eviction configuration, and actual retry/atomicity/duplicate-protection guarantees. The lesson provides no specific recovery implementation or universal product guarantees; these require chosen-product verification.

evidence.quote: A write can finish and its reply can be lost.
Replacing a value with the identical value twice does this if no other write intervenes.
Executing an increment twice adds twice, even if each increment is individually atomic.
A request ID alone is insufficient: recording it and changing the data must be coordinated atomically, with duplicate records retained for the retry window.
An entry can disappear before its TTL; a TTL is not a promise to retain it until the deadline.
Neither removal mechanism fetches a fresh replacement.
Expiration is also not a scheduler promising that business work runs at the exact deadline.

answers.answer: A data partition is a portion of keyspace assigned to a storage node or group. Distributing different key groups spreads storage and request work across their serving resources for many-key workloads. If most work targets one hot key, additional partitions may leave that key serving the same disproportionate demand, so measure request distribution and its serving capacity. A lagging replica is a maintained copy whose read may omit the successful write if the read mode allows staleness; that concerns read consistency. Durability instead asks whether acknowledged data survives specified failures. A durable write can be invisible to a lagging reader, while a visible new value does not prove crash survival. Verify implementation, selected read/write modes, replication and persistence settings, and explicit freshness and failure-survival guarantees before promising latest reads or survival. More nodes or a successful acknowledgment alone prove neither. The lesson supplies no universal mode or vendor guarantee to assume.

evidence.quote: A portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group.
More partitions alone may not help when most work still targets that key's serving capacity.
if it lags and the read mode permits stale results, it can return an older value after a successful write.
A durable write can still be absent from a lagging read. Conversely, seeing a new value does not prove that it will survive a crash.
Check the implementation, persistence and replication settings, and the selected read/write mode.

answers.answer: A fits directly: its known account key retrieves the independent preferences without discovering matches through a scan, and the record can be replaced as a whole. B needs more than basic lookup: scans for changing field filters read extra records; indexes consume storage and update work, and application-side joins add requests and coordination. A store with richer query or transaction support may fit B better, regardless of labels. For A, first verify atomic concurrent-update protection: two requests editing preferences read from the same older version could otherwise overwrite one another; an atomic version condition lets the loser reread and recompute. Second verify durability for required preferences: if this is the authoritative copy, an acknowledged update must survive the failures the service promises to handle, which depends on persistence and failure guarantees. The access model alone establishes neither fast nor safe service. Network, value sizes, hot keys and implementation limits affect latency and capacity; representative requests and failures must be measured, and other required authorization, retry, freshness, retention and outage behaviors checked.

evidence.quote: Independent records fetched and replaced by a known key are a direct fit.
Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.
The condition and the write must share the same atomic boundary.
Check the store's persistence settings and failure guarantees before using it as the only copy.
A known-key lookup can avoid unnecessary search, but network, value size, hot keys and implementation limits still affect latency and capacity.
